title: Per-layer kernel heatmap: long-context & MoE routing observations
body:
Summary

This note collects results from a set of microbenchmarks and traces focused on per-layer kernel behavior across Llama / Mistral / Qwen variants, with two stress dimensions: very long contexts (16k–32k tokens) and MoE routing (sparse experts). The novel piece here is a per-layer kernel heatmap (see attachment in linked PR) that maps which CUDA/CUTLASS/cuBLAS kernels the runtime picks for each transformer layer under realistic request mixtures. The heatmap highlights three recurring hotspots and actionable runtime changes.

Motivation
- We see intermittent latency spikes in long-context workloads and throughput drops for MoE models under multi-tenant load.
- Existing traces show that a large fraction of time is spent in a small set of kernels that differ by model family and layer index, but we lacked a layer-to-kernel map to reason about dynamic kernel selection.

What I ran
- Hardware: H100 (PCIe) and A100 40GB nodes. Two driver stacks: CUDA 12.2 / cuBLAS 12.x and CUTLASS-backed TF custom kernels.
- Models: llama-13B (Llama-architecture), mistral-7B-v2, qwen-7b. For MoE: a toy MoE variant built from llama-13B with 16 experts + top-1 gating (sparse weights from our model-onboarding branch).
- Workloads: single-request long-context (seq=16k, 24k, 32k) generating ~512 tokens; mixed-request multi-tenant profile (seq distribution: 512x3, 2k x6, 16k x1) to emulate bursty PLG traffic.
- Tools: nsys + CUPTI traces, custom kernel-logger hook in runtime (logs layer, chosen kernel, execution time, memory copies), nvtx annotations around routing operator.

Key observations (heatmap-style)
1) Layer-dependent kernel switching is common and repeatable
   - Llama: early layers (0..6) often use a CUTLASS GEMM kernel optimized for narrow batch/long sequence shapes; middle layers sometimes select cuBLAS GEMM_INT8 pathways when quantized; last layers switch to a different fused attention kernel because of larger head-dim accumulation.
   - Mistral: more consistent kernel footprints across layers — fewer switches — due to its attention layout (narrower FFN peak).
   - Qwen: frequent small-kernel launches for rotary embedding transforms; attention kernel selection flips when seq > 8k because of tiled attention tiling parameters.

2) MoE routing cost is not dominated by expert compute — it's routing overhead + memcpy + imbalance that kills throughput
   - Top-1 gating computes logits and a softmax, then gathers indices. The gating kernel itself is cheap (~2–4% of request time). But mmap/gather/permute to pack sub-batches for experts and the subsequent device-to-device memcpy (expert grouping) costs ~30–45% of the sparse forward path in our traces.
   - When experts are imbalanced, some CUDA streams finish early and wait on a single long expert; context switch/serialize overhead and kernel launch latency for the straggler expert inflates tail latency (90–99p).

3) Long-context interacts poorly with KV cache policies and kernel choice
   - For seq > 8k, attention kernels with O(N^2) memory patterns trigger different tiling and buffer allocation. On H100 we observed a spike in host->device staging allocations when the runtime falls back from fused attention to a more general kernel; these allocations add 8–12 ms per request.
   - Repeated prefix access (many requests share the same initial prefix) benefits from prefix grouping and memory aliasing — when we batch requests by prefix hash and reuse the same KV buffer, we reduce memcpy-bytes and see ~15–20% latency improvement on long seqs.

Micro numbers (representative)
- Llama-13B, seq=16k, gen 256 tokens on H100: average token time = 58ms, per-request latency = 3.2s. Heatmap shows: 48% time in attention GEMM kernels (two variants), 22% in KV memcpy/pack, 10% in ffn GEMMs, rest in kernel launch overhead + epilogue.
- MoE toy (16 experts), mixed-tenant run: effective throughput drops 28% under imbalance; routing+permute accounted for ~42% of the MoE forward path walltime.
- Qwen-7b, seq=8k: kernel switch at 8k -> average latency jump +12% due to different attention tiling producing more scatter/gather.

Interpretation
- Kernel selector policy currently uses a heuristic: (shape, dtype, seq) -> kernel id. That works for steady-state but misses cross-layer context (e.g., FFN shape vs attention tile interplay) and dynamic runtime conditions like multi-tenant memory pressure.
- MoE worst-case is not compute but data movement and scheduling. Our runtime should treat expert packing as a first-class schedulable unit with estimated cost and not a simple gather-then-dispatch.
- Long-context needs aggressive prefix-aware scheduling and memory aliasing to avoid repeated host/device moves and buffer re-allocation.

Concrete runtime changes to try (priority ordering)
1) Per-layer kernel affinity table (short-term)
   - During model load, run a fast microbenchmark per layer to produce a small table: preferred_kernel[layer_index] = (kernel_id, expected_peak_smem, workspace_bytes). Use as a default and fall back only if the kernel fails. This reduces flip-flopping during mixed workloads.
2) Expert pack scheduler (MoE) (mid-term)
   - Implement a scheduling stage that groups requests into sub-batches for each expert based on predicted cost, issues expert kernels on dedicated streams, and overlaps routing compute + memcpy where possible. Estimate memcpy cost and prefer route assignments that reduce peak cross-device copies.
3) Prefix grouping and KV aliasing (mid-term)
   - Add a prefix-hash based request coalescer in the runtime queue. If multiple pending requests share prefix hash, reuse the same KV buffer and enqueue their continuation tokens separately.
4) Kernel-selector telemetry and heatmap dashboard (low-effort)
   - Emit per-layer kernel choice metrics to Console: kernel_id, layer, seq_range bucket, percent of requests. Build a heatmap view so product/infra can see patterns over time.

Quick experiments suggested (next 2 weeks)
- Implement per-layer microbenchmarks in model loader and validate on a small model fleet. Track if default selection reduces cold-start flips. (INF-5127)
- Prototype simple expert-pack scheduler in a feature branch, run with synthetic imbalance patterns to validate tail-latency improvement target: reduce 95p by 20–30%.
- Run long-context prefix grouping on 1% of traffic for Llama-13B and measure host allocation stalls.

Open questions / risks
- Cost of microbenchmarking at model load — we add a small startup overhead. How does that interact with cold start SLOs? Consider async background microbenching and a conservative default.
- For MoE, some customers will want deterministic routing for compliance — dynamic scheduling may complicate that. Need an opt-in knob.
- Memory aliasing for KV is powerful but we must ensure we do not violate tenant isolation in Dedicated/Private modes.

Action items (owners)
- Maya: add per-layer microbench in the model loader (PR draft started in linked PR).
- Arjun: prototype expert-pack scheduler; create synthetic replay harness for imbalance cases (INF-5133).
- Samira: add heatmap telemetry schema to Console team and prototype a heatmap dashboard.
- Lucas: run extended A/B with prefix grouping on 1% Llama traffic and report latency tail changes.

Appendix: trace snippets & commands - nsys capture: nsys profile --trace=cuda,cudnn,osrt -o ~/trace_16k nsys_run.sh - kernel logger: runtime flag --emit-layer-kernel-log=/tmp/layer-kernels.log

Trace example (condensed)
[layer 0] kernel=cu_cutlass_sgemm_tiled tile=(128,64) time=7.8ms
[layer 1] kernel=cublasGemmEx_int8 time=3.2ms
[attention stage] kernel=fused_attention_v2 fallback=false time=45.4ms
[moe gate] kernel=gate_logits time=1.1ms
[moe pack] step=permute time=12.6ms memcpy=9.8ms

Notes for reviewers
- The attached PR contains the microbenchmark harness and a lightweight visualizer that renders the per-layer kernel heatmap (svg/png) used to build the observations above.
- Please focus review on: expected startup cost tradeoffs for microbenchmarks, API shape for the expert-pack scheduler, and telemetry fields that are safe to emit for private deployments.

End.
